summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 so a node can bind specific flows to specific care-of addresses. A multihomed device can tell its home agent and other mobility entities to send certain inbound traffic to particular addresses. It is a proposed standard and updates RFC 5648.

plainLanguage.summary:
Mobile IPv6 lets a device that is away from home keep its home address and forward traffic to a temporary address. This RFC adds a finer control: the device can send one kind of traffic to one temporary address and another kind to a different one.

The device states the rule in the binding update it already sends, and the network matches each arriving packet against those rules in order.

questions: how does a multihomed mobile node direct flows
what is mobile ipv6 flow binding
what is a flow identification mobility option
how does a mobile node send different flows to different care-of addresses
what is a bid in mobile ipv6
subtitle: Sending one kind of a mobile node's traffic to one address and the rest to another.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 binds a care-of address to a home address, and the older specifications let a mobile node register only one address at a time, so different kinds of traffic could not be sent to different addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a flow identification mobility option that names a traffic selector and the binding identifiers the matching packets should be forwarded to, plus a flow summary option for keeping existing bindings alive.
tldr.outcome: A multihomed mobile node can direct particular flows to particular care-of addresses without disturbing the others, and the home agent, correspondent node and mobility anchor point all forward matching packets accordingly. The document is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6089 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It extends Mobile IPv6, defined in RFC 3775, and Network Mobility Basic Support with the flow identification option, and it builds on the multiple care-of address work of RFC 5648.

sections.title: One Flow, One Care-of Address
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6, Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6 and Network Mobility Basic Support let a mobile node or mobile router manage its mobility with the binding update message, which binds one care-of address to one home address and its associated mobile networks. The binding update can go to the home agent, and in Mobile IPv6 also to a correspondent node or to a mobility anchor point. The semantics of the binding update are limited to care-of address changes: those specifications do not let a mobile node bind more than one address to the home address. RFC 5648 extended them to allow more than one care-of address for one home address.

This document extends them further, so that each binding can carry a policy. A policy can ask for special treatment of a particular flow, where a flow is a group of packets matching a traffic selector. The result is that a mobile node can bind a particular flow to a care-of address without affecting the other flows that use the same home address, and it can bind a flow to a care-of address directly with the correspondent node and the mobility agents, the home agent and the mobility anchor point.

The document defines a flow as a set of IP packets matching a traffic selector. A traffic selector can identify the source and destination IP addresses, the transport protocol number, the source and destination port numbers, and other fields in the IP and higher-layer headers. The document does not define traffic selectors themselves, which other specifications do; it defines the format of the sub-option that carries them.

With the flow identifier option, a mobile node can bind one or more flows to a care-of address while keeping the other flows on another care-of address. The mobile node builds its flow binding requests from local policies, link characteristics and the types of applications running at the time; those policies are out of scope.

The flow identification mobility option can be attached to any binding update, whether it goes to a mobility agent or to a correspondent node.

The RFC notes that per-packet load balancing is not envisioned here, because it can disturb TCP congestion avoidance, which wants the packets of one connection to keep their order, and it can affect real-time connections through varying round-trip times, and it interferes with traffic that has anti-replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IPv6 lets a device that is away from home keep its home address and forward traffic to a temporary address. This RFC adds a finer control: the device can send one kind of traffic to one temporary address and another kind to a different one.

sections.title: Flows, Selectors and Bindings
sections.content: Four terms do the work. A flow is a sequence of packets for which the mobile node wants special handling from the home agent, the correspondent node or the mobility anchor point. A traffic selector is one or more parameters that can be matched against fields in the packet headers to classify it, for example the source and destination IP addresses, the transport protocol number, the source and destination port numbers, and other fields in the IP and higher-layer headers. A flow binding consists of a traffic selector and one or more binding identifiers, and packets that match the selector are forwarded to the care-of addresses named by those identifiers. A flow identifier uniquely identifies a flow binding for a mobile node; it is generated by the mobile node and cached in the table of flow binding entries kept by the mobile node, the home agent, the correspondent node or the mobility anchor point.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is a group of packets that should be treated alike. The rule that picks them out is the traffic selector, and the flow binding is the selector plus the addresses the matching packets should go to.

sections.title: The Flow Identification Mobility Option
sections.content:
The flow identification mobility option is a new mobility option, carried in the binding update and acknowledgement messages. It holds the information that lets the receiver install a policy on a traffic flow and route it to a given care-of address, and several of these options may appear in the same binding update. The alignment requirement for the option is 2n.

The option starts with an Option Type field, which Section 4.2 sets to 45, an Option Len field, and a 16-bit FID field holding the unique identifier of the flow binding. The FID is used to refer to an existing flow binding or to create a new one, and it is set by the mobile node; the value zero is reserved and MUST NOT be used. The FID-PRI field is a 16-bit priority that decides which policy runs when two flow descriptions overlap, and a lower number means a higher priority. The value zero is reserved, and the FID-PRI MUST be unique among the flows of a given mobile node.

The Status field is an 8-bit value that says whether the flow binding operation succeeded for the flow in that option. It only means something in a Binding Acknowledgement and must be ignored in a binding update. The values reserved are zero for a successful flow binding, 128 for administratively prohibited, 129 for a rejection with no reason given, 130 for a malformed option, 131 when the binding identifier is not found, 132 when the flow identifier is not found, and 133 when the traffic selector format is not supported.

After that come optional sub-options in a type-length-value format. The sub-option type is an 8-bit value, and a receiver that does not recognise it MUST silently ignore it and carry on with the rest of the option. The sub-option length is an 8-bit value that gives the length of the sub-option without the type and length fields, except that sub-option type zero, Pad1, has no length field at all. Four sub-option types are defined: Pad1, type zero, which inserts one octet of padding; PadN, type one, which inserts two or more octets of padding; the binding reference sub-option, type two, which lists the binding identifiers that the flow is associated with; and the traffic selector sub-option, type three, which carries the selector itself.

The binding reference sub-option holds one or more 16-bit binding identifiers, so the number of identifiers is the length field divided by two. When a flow is bound with this sub-option, the binding identifier mobility option of RFC 5648 MUST be in the same binding update or an earlier one.

The traffic selector sub-option holds a Traffic Selector Format byte, whose value zero is reserved, a reserved byte that MUST be set to zero, and the selector itself, whose format and content are out of scope for this document; the selector defined in RFC 6088 is the one that MUST be implemented.

Note that the registry list in Section 8 of the same document gives the two option type numbers the other way round: it names 44 as the flow identification option and 45 as the flow summary option, while Sections 4.2 and 4.2.2 give them 45 and 44.
sections.plainLanguage: The new option names the rule and the addresses it applies to. Each rule has a number of its own, a priority, and a place to report whether it worked.

sections.title: The Flow Bindings List
sections.content:
The binding cache defined in Mobile IPv6 holds the mobile node's home address, its registered care-of addresses and the lifetime of the binding, and RFC 5648 extended it to hold more than one care-of address, each with a binding identifier. This document does not change the binding cache further.

The flow bindings are a separate conceptual list, with one entry for each registered flow binding. An entry points at a binding cache entry through its binding identifier, and it holds the flow identifier, the traffic selector, the list of binding identifiers, an active or inactive flag, and the FID-PRI that breaks ties between overlapping bindings.

For a given mobile node the flow identifier MUST identify one entry, so a mobile node can have only one entry with a given identifier at a time. The list is ordered by FID-PRI, and a valid binding identifier is needed for an entry to be active. If all the binding identifiers of an entry are deregistered the entry becomes inactive and stops affecting data traffic; if only some are still valid, the invalid ones are simply ignored.

Every node that keeps flow bindings keeps an ordered list of care-of addresses for that mobile node, built from the BID-PRI field of the binding identifier mobility option. A packet that matches no flow binding SHOULD be forwarded to the care-of address with the highest priority, the one with the lowest BID-PRI value.

The RFC's example shows a table of three entries: a TCP entry with priority 10 that is active and points at one care-of address, an entry for a source address with priority 30 that is inactive because its binding identifier no longer exists, and a UDP entry with priority 40 that is active and points at two care-of addresses. All TCP traffic matches the first entry and goes to the second care-of address; any UDP traffic that does not match earlier entries matches the third and is replicated to two care-of addresses; anything left over goes to the care-of address with the highest priority.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mobile node has a list of rules, ordered by priority. A packet is matched against them in order, and the first rule that matches decides where the packet goes. A rule whose care-of address has gone away is skipped.

sections.title: What the Mobile Node Sends
sections.content:
The list of flow bindings kept by the home agent, the correspondent node or the mobility anchor point is controlled by the mobile node through the flow identification and flow summary options in its binding updates. Each update can add, modify, refresh or delete a binding, and more than one flow identification option may be in the same update, but each must have a different flow identifier.

All flow binding state MUST be refreshed in every binding update the mobile node sends, and any previously registered flow binding that is not included in an update is deleted. So bindings that are to be kept but not changed have to be listed in a flow summary option.

To add a new binding, the mobile node sends a flow identification option whose FID is not already in the receiver's list. The care-of addresses the option refers to must be registered by that same update or registered earlier. The FID-PRI field sets the position of the new entry in the list, and the Status field is zero in every binding update. The option MUST include exactly one traffic selector sub-option, with the format field set to the non-zero value the mobile node uses, and exactly one binding reference sub-option.

To modify an existing binding, the mobile node sends a flow identification option with an FID that is already in the list. It may leave out the traffic selector to keep the one already registered, and it may leave out the binding reference to keep the identifiers already registered. A binding can also be changed without touching the entry, by changing the care-of address behind a binding identifier, which is the procedure of RFC 5648.

To refresh a binding without changing it, the mobile node sends a flow summary option listing its flow identifier. Each flow summary option can identify up to 127 identifiers, so more than one may be needed, and a given identifier SHOULD NOT appear more than once. Inactive bindings have to be refreshed as well, or they are removed.

Removal is implicit: a binding is removed simply by leaving its identifier out of the update. A binding can also be made inactive by removing the binding identifiers behind it, without removing the binding itself. When all of them are gone the binding MUST be marked inactive, so its state is kept but it no longer affects traffic, and the mobile node can bring it back by associating it with valid identifiers again.

Deregistration in the Mobile IPv6 style deletes all the bindings, including the flow bindings. A home registration in the RFC 5648 style is treated like any other link, associated with a binding identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile node keeps the receiver's list up to date by sending its whole list every time. Anything left out is dropped. A new rule carries the selector and the addresses to use; an existing rule can be changed or just repeated to keep it alive.

sections.title: Matching Packets and Forwarding Them
sections.content:
These rules do not change the packet interception rules of Mobile IPv6 and Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6. They apply to home agents, mobility anchor points and correspondent nodes as part of the routing process for any packet addressed to a valid home address of the mobile node, and for nodes other than correspondent nodes also to packets addressed under any of the registered prefixes, for IPv6 and for IPv4.

Before a packet is forwarded to the mobile node it MUST be matched against the ordered list of flow bindings for that mobile node. A match is attempted with the traffic selector in the first, highest, entry, and the first entry that creates a match decides how the packet is routed. When a packet matches, a copy is forwarded to each care-of address named by the binding identifiers on that line.

If one of the identifiers does not point to a valid care-of address, for example because it was deregistered, that identifier has no effect and the packet goes to the remaining care-of addresses. If none of them is valid the entry is inactive and is skipped.

A packet that matches no active entry SHOULD be forwarded to the care-of address with the highest priority, the one with the lowest BID-PRI.

Fragmented packets need care: only the first fragment carries the transport layer headers, so later fragments may not match the same selector. Home agents, mobility anchor points and correspondent nodes SHOULD forward all the fragments of a packet the same way, following the match of the first fragment. The details of how that is achieved are implementation specific and are not defined in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each arriving packet is compared with the rules in order. The first rule that matches sends copies of the packet to the addresses that rule names. Packets that match nothing go to the highest-priority address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new option adds granularity to the binding update and acknowledgement messages, so it inherits the security considerations of those documents. Since the flow identification option is part of the mobility header, it uses the same security as the binding update, whether that goes to a mobility agent or to a correspondent node.

The document does not open new fundamental lines of attack, but it allows attacks of a finer granularity than those on the binding update itself. An attacker who can impersonate the mobile node or modify a binding update can divert or replicate flows of particular interest to an address of the attacker's choosing. That makes it doubly critical that authentication and integrity services are applied to binding updates.

One point about the optional anti-replay feature of ESP: when packets to and from different care-of addresses travel on the same security association, some packets could be discarded at the receiver because of the windowing mechanism. A sender SHOULD therefore put traffic to and from different care-of addresses, but with the same home address in the selector values, on different security associations. To allow that, the IPsec implementation SHOULD maintain several security associations between the same sender and receiver with the same selectors, and the distribution of traffic among them is decided locally by the sender and is not negotiated by IKEv2.
sections.plainLanguage: The finer control means an attacker who can fake a binding update can now redirect just the traffic they care about, so the protection of binding updates matters even more.

fields.name: Option Type
fields.desc: The mobility option type. Section 4.2 of the RFC sets it to 45.

fields.name: Option Len
fields.desc: Length of the option in octets.

fields.name: FID
fields.desc: The unique identifier of the flow binding, set by the mobile node. Zero is reserved.

fields.name: FID-PRI
fields.desc: Priority of this option. A lower number means a higher priority, and it must be unique per mobile node.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Unused. Must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Status
fields.desc: The result of the flow binding operation. It only means something in an acknowledgement.

viz.caption: THE STATUS CODES OF THE FLOW IDENTIFICATION OPTION

items.label: Administratively prohibited
items.desc: The receiver will not maintain flow bindings.

items.label: Rejected, reason unspecified
items.desc: The binding was refused without a reason.

items.label: Option malformed
items.desc: The flow identification option could not be parsed.

items.label: BID not found
items.desc: The binding identifier behind the flow does not exist.

items.label: FID not found
items.desc: The flow identifier is not in the receiver's list.

items.label: Traffic selector format not supported
items.desc: The receiver cannot use the selector that was sent.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TERMS THIS RFC ADDS

items.title: Flow
items.text: A sequence of packets that the mobile node wants treated in a special way.

items.title: Traffic selector
items.text: The parameters compared with the packet header to decide whether a packet belongs to the flow.

items.title: Flow binding
items.text: A traffic selector plus the binding identifiers whose care-of addresses the matching packets go to.

items.title: Flow identifier
items.text: The number that names one flow binding for one mobile node.
